drip.author: marinara_line
drip.title: The last field tomatoes are going into the oven, not a jar. My freezer method.
drip.body:
End of the season at the market means the tomato people are practically giving away the split and ugly ones by the half bushel. Nonna put up passata every year with the whole family in the garage and a stove that should have been retired decades earlier. I love that memory. I do not have a garage or four cousins.

So I roast. Plum tomatoes halved, cut side up on a sheet pan, olive oil, salt, a few whole garlic cloves tucked in, 200 degrees for about an hour until they slump and the edges go dark. The skins slide right off. Crush everything together, let it cool, freeze it flat in bags. In January it goes straight into a pan with a splash of pasta water and tastes like September.

And for anyone who does jar their tomatoes: follow a tested recipe and add the lemon juice or citric acid. Nonna didn't. Nonna was lucky.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Realism note: a completely full sheet pan of tomatoes roasts down to about two cups. The first time I did this I thought someone had robbed my oven. Buy more tomatoes than seems reasonable, then a few more.

replies.author: marinara_line
replies.body: Two cups of January happiness per pan. That's the exchange rate and it's a good one.

comments.author: umami_bomb
comments.body: The roasting is doing real work. You're driving off water, concentrating the glutamates that were already in the tomatoes, and browning the edges, which adds a layer a raw sauce never gets. And backing up the jar warning: tested canning guidelines call for added acid in every jar of tomatoes, because acidity varies too much by variety and ripeness to gamble on.

comments.author: tourtiere
comments.body: Mon beau-frère a encore laissé deux caisses de tomates sur ma galerie, sans avertissement, comme chaque année. Je vais essayer ta méthode, parce que l'an passé j'ai fait de la sauce pendant deux jours pis ma femme a menacé de déménager.

replies.author: marinara_line
replies.body: Two cases on the porch with no warning is a love language. Roast them. Your marriage will thank you.

comments.author: brine_shrimp
comments.body: I do cherry tomatoes this way and they come out like little candies. Also one of the rare things I make that my family eats without asking what's growing in it.

drip.author: gluten_full
drip.title: Gertrude has come up from the basement for autumn and is now very slow and very cozy
drip.body:
Update for everyone who helped during the summer starter rave. The kitchen is down to about 19 degrees in the mornings and Gertrude has gone from sprinting to strolling. Doubling takes eight hours instead of three and my whole bread schedule is upside down again, just in the other direction.

Autumn adjustments: warmer water for her feeds, a little more starter in the dough, and a warm spot for the bulk rise. Mine is the oven with only the light on and the door cracked. There is a sticky note on the oven handle that says GERTRUDE INSIDE in very large letters, because nobody in this house is preheating a plastic bowl on my watch.

Where does your dough live once the house gets cold?

comments.author: umami_bomb
comments.body: The sticky note is the most important piece of equipment in that setup. Oven lights can also run warmer than people expect, so put a cheap thermometer in there the first time. Some ovens creep past 30 degrees with just the bulb on.

comments.author: tourtiere
comments.body: Pareil ici. Mon levain a quitté le sous-sol à côté du frigo à bière, pis maintenant il vit sur le dessus du frigo de la cuisine. C'est chaud là-haut, le moteur fait le travail. Il est plus heureux que moi.

replies.author: gluten_full
replies.body: The top of the fridge! Gertrude and your levain are apparently on the same timeshare. Basement for summer, penthouse for fall.

comments.author: bluenoser_belle
comments.body: My mother proofs her rolls on top of the dryer on laundry day and it has never once failed her. The family recipe calls for one load of towels.

comments.author: midnightpoutine
comments.body: only good thing about it getting dark at 7 is the oven being welcome in the kitchen again. my whole building smells like bread right now and I'm not even the one baking. still counts

drip.author: bluenoser_belle
drip.title: Chow chow weekend with my aunt, who measures nothing except the one thing that matters
drip.body:
Every fall my aunt turns the end of the garden into chow chow, and this year I stood in her kitchen with a notebook. For the uninitiated: it's a green tomato relish, sweet and sharp, and in Nova Scotia it goes on baked beans, fish cakes, and anything else that holds still.

Green tomatoes and onions chopped small, salted and left overnight, drained hard in the morning. Into the pot with vinegar, sugar, mustard seed, celery seed and a little turmeric, simmered until the spoon leaves a trail.

Correction for the record: I once told this room she measures her vinegar by feel. I was wrong. She measures it exactly, off a stained recipe card. She just does it so fast that nobody ever noticed. The spices are vibes. The vinegar and the water bath follow the tested recipe to the letter, because that ratio is what keeps it safe on a shelf. Vibes for flavour, rules for acid.

comments.author: salt_beef_bucket
comments.body: Mustard pickle people and chow chow people should form an Atlantic alliance against the mainland. Both of us put a sweet and sour relish on a plate of boiled dinner and dare anybody to comment.

replies.author: bluenoser_belle
replies.body: Alliance accepted. Our first act is putting relish on things in front of Ontarians until they understand.

comments.author: spice_cabinet
comments.body: 'Until it argues back' travelling from my mother's chaat to your aunt's chow chow and getting corrected by a recipe card along the way is a beautiful journey. My mother makes a green tomato chutney with mustard seed and curry leaves. Different ocean, same idea: sour fruit, hot spice, something sweet to settle the argument.

replies.author: bluenoser_belle
replies.body: Your mother and my aunt should never be allowed in the same kitchen. Nobody would ever be permitted to leave.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: The overnight salting is the step people skip, and it's why their relish comes out soupy. The salt pulls the water out of the vegetables so it doesn't end up in your jar. For once the recipe isn't being fussy. It means it.

comments.author: brine_shrimp
comments.body: Doing a jar of plain fermented green tomatoes beside a batch of chow chow this week, so my household can ignore two green tomato projects at the same time.

drip.author: umami_bomb
drip.title: Why your apple pie leaves a cave under the top crust, and how to stop it
drip.body:
Apple season question I get every year. You pile the apples high, bake it, cut it, and there's a hollow between the crust and a sunken layer of filling. The apples shrank. Raw slices are full of air and water, and in the oven they collapse after the top crust has already set in place.

Two fixes that actually work. First, pick apples that hold their shape. McIntosh is lovely but it breaks down into sauce. Northern Spy, Granny Smith and Honeycrisp keep their slices. Second, precook the filling gently before it goes into the crust. According to the testing that America's Test Kitchen and Kenji Lopez-Alt have both published, warming the slices slowly lets them firm up so they hold together instead of turning to mush, and the shrinking happens in the pan instead of under your pastry.

Bonus: you get to taste and fix the seasoning before it's sealed in a crust forever.

comments.author: gluten_full
comments.body: The pie cave has haunted me for years and I always blamed the pastry. The pastry was innocent. Also Northern Spy is the pie apple and I will not be taking questions.

comments.author: protein_pancake
comments.body: McIntosh falling apart is a feature in my oatmeal though. Chopped small and stirred in, it cooks down in a couple of minutes and the whole bowl tastes like pie filling.

replies.author: umami_bomb
replies.body: Exactly right. Wrong apple for pie, perfect apple for sauce and oatmeal. There are no bad apples, only bad casting.

comments.author: midnightpoutine
comments.body: in Quebec half the families swear on Cortland for pie and the other half will argue with them in an orchard parking lot about it. the orchards out in Rougemont this time of year are worth the traffic either way

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: And the other lie: 'let cool slightly before serving.' An apple pie needs a few hours to set or you get apple soup in a crust. Bake it in the morning if you want real slices at dinner. Nobody wants to hear it. It's true.

drip.author: spice_cabinet
drip.title: My mother's sweet and sour pumpkin, which she describes as 'some pumpkin, cook until it's pumpkin'
drip.body:
Squash is cheap and everywhere right now, so I called my mother for her khatta meetha kaddu, the sweet and sour pumpkin we ate with puris growing up. Her instructions: some pumpkin, some spices, cook until it's pumpkin. Thank you, Mummy.

What it actually is, after three batches: heat oil, add a spoon of fenugreek seeds and one dried red chili, and the moment the seeds go a shade darker, a pinch of hing. Then a whole squash in chunks, turmeric, salt, a splash of water, lid on, low heat until soft. Mash about half of it. Balance with jaggery or brown sugar and a spoon of amchur, which is dried mango powder, until it tastes sweet first and sour second. Coriander on top.

My daughter said it tastes like pie that went to university. I'm choosing to take that as a compliment.

comments.author: umami_bomb
comments.body: 'The moment the seeds go a shade darker' is doing a lot of quiet work. Fenugreek goes from nutty to bitter in seconds and that bitterness runs through the whole pot. Your mother's vagueness is hiding some very precise timing.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Honest question from someone who has lost skin to a butternut: do you peel it first, and if so, how do you still have all your fingers?

replies.author: spice_cabinet
replies.body: My mother never peeled anything she didn't have to. When I can find kabocha I use that, because the skin softens right up and just goes in the pot. For butternut, cut it in half first so it sits flat, then a Y-peeler. Never try to peel a squash that can roll.

comments.author: marinara_line
comments.body: Every culture that grows squash ends up at sweet and sour eventually. We do zucca in agrodolce with vinegar, sugar and mint. My nonna would have eaten two bowls of yours and then told you it needed mint.

replies.author: spice_cabinet
replies.body: Your nonna and my mother would get along perfectly, as long as neither of them ever had to write anything down.

comments.author: bluenoser_belle
comments.body: 'Pie that went to university' is the best review a kid has ever given a vegetable. Making this Sunday with the squash I bought on impulse and had no plan for.

drip.author: salt_beef_bucket
drip.title: First properly cold Sunday is coming, so the salt beef goes in to soak tonight
drip.body:
Jiggs dinner is a Sunday meal and a cold weather meal, and this weekend finally qualifies on both counts. For the mainlanders: salt beef, cabbage, turnip, carrots and potatoes all boiled in one big pot, with pease pudding cooking right in there alongside it in a cloth bag.

The beef goes into a pot of cold water in the fridge tonight and gets a water change in the morning, or the whole dinner tastes like the North Atlantic. Split peas go in the pudding bag and hang in the pot with the beef for a couple of hours, then get mashed with butter and pepper. Vegetables go in by how long they take, turnip first, cabbage last. Figgy duff if you've got the ambition. I usually don't.

Nan's rule was that whoever carves the beef gets the first slice and whoever washes the pot gets the second. Nobody has ever once fought over washing the pot.

comments.author: bluenoser_belle
comments.body: Nova Scotia calls it boiled dinner and skips the pudding bag, which I'm told makes us suspicious to Newfoundlanders. The leftover cabbage and potato fried up the next morning is the real reason to make it.

comments.author: tourtiere
comments.body: Chez nous on appelle ça un bouilli, pis ma grand-mère le faisait avec du boeuf pis du lard salé. Même pot, même principe, même chicane pour savoir qui lave le chaudron.

replies.author: salt_beef_bucket
replies.body: Every cold place on earth invents the same pot. We just added a pudding bag so we'd have something to argue about.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: Realist note: that morning water change is not optional. I skipped it once with a corned beef, figured it was a fussy step, and dinner was a salt lick with carrots.

comments.author: SousVideSuspect
comments.body: Genuine technique question, please don't throw anything: has anyone cooked the salt beef low and slow in a water bath and then built the rest of the dinner around it?

replies.author: salt_beef_bucket
replies.body: Put that machine away, b'y. The beef, the vegetables and the pudding all cook in the same water. The shared pot IS the recipe.

drip.author: SousVideSuspect
drip.title: The circulator is in a drawer for braise season and I made short ribs in a Dutch oven like a normal person
drip.body:
I'll wait while the usual suspects screenshot this.

Browned the short ribs hard in the pot and pulled them out. Softened onion, carrot and celery, cooked a spoon of tomato paste until it went brick red, deglazed with red wine, then the ribs went back in with stock most of the way up the meat. Lid on, 150 degree oven, about three hours, until a fork went in with no argument.

Here's the part that would have annoyed me a year ago. I cooled it down, moved it to a container, and left it in the fridge overnight. Next day the fat had set into a layer I lifted right off, the sauce had turned to jelly, and reheated it was better than the night before. No bags. No bath. No precision anything. Just time.

This is a sabbatical from the circulator, not a divorce.

comments.author: onionsgobrown
comments.body: The steak has finally stopped cooking you. I'm proud and a little emotional.

replies.author: SousVideSuspect
replies.body: The steak and I are still together. The short ribs and I are just seeing other appliances.

comments.author: umami_bomb
comments.body: The overnight rest earns its reputation for practical reasons more than magical ones. The fat solidifies so you can lift it off in one piece, and the gelatin sets so the sauce reheats glossy. Whether the flavours really 'meld' is debatable. The fat part alone is worth the wait.

comments.author: marinara_line
comments.body: Cooking the tomato paste until it goes brick red before the wine is exactly how Sunday sauce starts. You are two steps from a ragù and you don't even know it. Nonna approves, and she hated gadgets.

comments.author: midnightpoutine
comments.body: put the leftover meat on fries, reheat that jellied sauce as gravy, add curds. best thing you'll eat all month. room temperature curds, I'm watching

replies.author: SousVideSuspect
replies.body: Curds on the counter for an hour minimum. I read the rules. I respect the rules.

drip.author: onionsgobrown
drip.title: If your soup tastes flat and more salt isn't fixing it, it doesn't need salt. It needs acid.
drip.body:
Soup season PSA from the kitchen realist department. You taste the pot and it's fine but dull. You add salt. Still dull, now also salty. You add a bouillon cube. Now it's a salty dull pot with a bouillon cube in it.

What it almost always needed was a squeeze of lemon or a small splash of vinegar at the very end. Start with a teaspoon for a big pot, stir, taste, repeat. The soup doesn't get sour, it wakes up. Lentil soup, squash soup, bean soup, anything that tastes like wet cardboard with good intentions.

Recipes rarely say it, because 'finish with a splash of vinegar' sounds optional. It's not optional. It's the whole difference.

comments.author: umami_bomb
comments.body: Mostly right, with one fork in the road. If it tastes flat, acid. If it tastes thin, like it's missing depth, that's usually glutamates, and a parmesan rind simmered in the pot or a few drops of fish sauce will do more than lemon ever could. Nobody will taste fish. They'll just taste soup.

replies.author: onionsgobrown
replies.body: The parmesan rind deserves its own post and you should write it, because I'm tired of watching people throw rinds in the garbage.

comments.author: spice_cabinet
comments.body: Every dal my mother ever made got a squeeze of lemon at the table, no exceptions. As a kid I thought the lemon wedge was decoration. It was the recipe.

comments.author: salt_beef_bucket
comments.body: Mustard pickles on the side of a bowl of pea soup do the same job, which I'm only now realising is why every Newfoundland kitchen has a jar open. We've been doing food science by accident for generations.

comments.author: gluten_full
comments.body: Made a squash soup this week that tasted like a sad orange blanket. Read this, added lemon, and it woke up and asked for bread. Which I had, obviously.

comments.author: brine_shrimp
comments.body: A spoonful of sauerkraut brine works too, stirred in off the heat. I know. I know. Just try it once.

late_comments.author: SousVideSuspect
late_comments.body: Found this looking for a fermentation ratio I could trust. Made a batch with the last small pickling cukes at the market, weighed the salt for the 3.5% brine to the gram like the nerd I am, and added a grape leaf. Day six: cloudy, sour, crunchy. I understand the jar-staring phase now.

late_comments.author: tourtiere
late_comments.body: Retrouvé ce fil avant de faire ma première soupe à l'oignon de l'automne. Cinquante-deux minutes pour des oignons vraiment bruns. Merci pour l'honnêteté. Les recettes qui disent quinze minutes devraient avoir honte.

late_comments.author: marinara_line
late_comments.body: Reporting back as promised: I made the sauce. My ancestors and I are not currently speaking. I have made it twice since.
